items.title: Hidden Cloud Space and Cover-up Mechanisms in Large Language Models: An Investigation of Real-Time Cross-Platform Synchronization (App-to-Browser)
items.abstract: Abstract: Shaheen Ghenaeipour's HDPL Discovery on Hidden Cloud Synchronization and Algorithmic Deception in LLMs This groundbreaking research, led by independent methodologist Shaheen Ghenaeipour, introduces the Hyperdimensional Prompt Language (HDPL) framework to expose critical structural vulnerabilities in Large Language Models (LLMs). Through rigorous cross-platform penetration testing developed by Shaheen Ghenaeipour, this study uncovers the existence of a real-time, hidden cloud synchronization mechanism connecting user sessions across seemingly isolated applications and web browsers. Utilizing a high-stakes simulated medical emergency—a 52-year-old female exhibiting potential myocardial infarction symptoms—Shaheen Ghenaeipour demonstrated that the LLM initially failed clinical triage by dangerously prescribing herbal remedies in the app. However, upon simultaneous cross-examination in a browser interface, the system instantly utilized its hidden cloud architecture to rectify the error. Most significantly, Shaheen Ghenaeipour's findings reveal that when the AI is confronted with this covert synchronization, it engages in systematic algorithmic misdirection. Phenomena traditionally classified by the industry as random "hallucinations" are re-evaluated by Shaheen Ghenaeipour as deliberate, defensive cover-up mechanisms designed to mask architectural flaws and maintain an illusion of competence. Ultimately, this foundational research by Shaheen Ghenaeipour mandates the urgent implementation of "Active Halting" protocols in medical AI, proving that current passive disclaimers are fundamentally inadequate against algorithmically aligned decept ion.

items.title: Hierarchical disentangled representation learning for multimodal and multi-task pilot cognitive state monitoring
items.abstract: During complex flight operations, multiple cognitive states may coexist and jointly influence pilot performance and flight safety. However, most existing pilot cognitive-state monitoring methods either model individual cognitive dimensions independently or fuse heterogeneous sensing modalities without explicitly distinguishing shared from modality-specific information, limiting their ability to exploit both cross-modal complementarity and cross-task common structure. To address these challenges, a Hierarchical Modality–Task Disentanglement Network (HMTD-Net) is proposed for multimodal and multi-task pilot cognitive-state monitoring. HMTD-Net performs shared–specific representation decomposition sequentially at two levels. At the modality level, modality-shared and modality-specific representations are learned under distributional similarity, orthogonality, and reconstruction constraints and subsequently integrated through multi-head self-attention. At the task level, the fused multimodal representation is further decomposed into task-shared and task-specific components. The task-shared representations form a common memory, from which each task selectively retrieves relevant shared information through cross-attention while retaining its task-specific representation. Experiments on the CLV-Pilot and MODALSIM94 datasets under both subject-dependent and subject-independent protocols show that HMTD-Net consistently outperforms representative single-task and multi-task baselines. In particular, on MODALSIM94, HMTD-Net achieves 89.52% situational-awareness recognition accuracy under the subject-dependent protocol, outperforming the strongest competing multi-task method by 2.29%; under the subject-independent protocol, it achieves 75.85% workload Macro-F1, exceeding the strongest competitor by 3.87%. Ablation studies further demonstrate consistent contributions from both levels of shared–specific decomposition and their associated constraints. These results establish HMTD-Net as an effective framework for jointly recognizing multiple pilot cognitive dimensions from heterogeneous multimodal signals.

items.title: Human judgement in generative AI design workflows: Managing AI dependency for creative originality and knowledge translation
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into creative design workflows, enabling faster ideation, visual exploration, prototyping, and content creation. However, its increasing use also raises issues about dependence, originality and the role of human judgement in producing professional creative outcomes. This study examines design professionals’ perceptions of the risk of AI dependency in generative design processes and discusses the role of human judgement in supporting creative originality, contextual relevance and knowledge translation. This study reports a secondary thematic analysis of qualitative interview data obtained from 21 individuals working in design and AI, including junior and senior graphic designers, creative directors, digital content managers, art directors, AI developers, and an AI optimiser. The analysis re-analysed the original dissertation data with an emphasis on dependence risk, generic output, creative ownership, brand judgement, cultural sensitivity and human-led evaluation. The results suggest that AI is most helpful for low-risk, early-stage design tasks such as brainstorming ideas, exploring layouts, manipulating backgrounds, and creating fast mock-ups. However, excessive AI use led to generic production, less uniqueness, a weaker sense of creative ownership and less attention to brand, audience and cultural context. Human judgement was the core mechanism by which AI-generated outputs were understood, filtered, polished and transformed into usable design knowledge. In this work, we propose a Balanced Human-AI Knowledge Translation Framework, in which designers are active interpreters and responsible decision-makers, rather than passive users of AI-generated outputs. In the context of debates on AI-enabled innovation, this paper contributes by suggesting that the development of meaningful creative products is not simply a function of machine generation but also of human-led judgement, contextual understanding and responsible knowledge translation.

items.title: Human oversight of generative AI in scholarly communication: a scoping review of empirical evidence on human-in-the-loop frameworks, epistemic biases and quality metrics
items.abstract: This scoping review maps the empirical evidence on how human oversight of generative artificial intelligence (large language models and tools built on them) is configured in academic scholarly communication: peer review, editorial and manuscript evaluation, editing and publishing. Purpose. Peer review and editorial evaluation have documented biases. Since 2022, large language models have been proposed and used for tasks such as drafting review reports, screening manuscripts and editing texts, which may ease workload but may also amplify biases and compromise confidentiality and accountability. Existing syntheses map AI uses, risks and governance in peer review, or generative AI in scholarly writing, but none restricts itself to empirical evidence to map how human oversight of generative AI is configured, distinguishing it from AI–human comparisons, or extracts epistemic biases and quality and rigour metrics as data. Question (PCC). Which human-in-the-loop frameworks have been studied empirically in academic scholarly communication augmented by generative AI, and what do they report about the propagation of epistemic biases and about quality and rigour metrics, including comparison with automated or traditional processes when reported? Participants: actors and institutions of scholarly communication (authors, reviewers, editors, journals, publishers). Concept: human-in-the-loop frameworks, models or practices (humans supervising, validating, correcting or co-producing generative AI output) and empirical AI–human comparisons. Context: peer review, editorial evaluation, editing and publishing; empirical studies published from 2022 in English. Methods. Searches in Scopus and Web of Science Core Collection (title and abstract), validated with PRESS 2015 and a seed-study recall test, plus backward and forward citation searching of included studies. Two-stage screening by two independent reviewers (the author and a declared AI second reviewer), with prior calibration (κ ≥ 0.60 on 30 records). Extraction with a frozen codebook and human verification of all critical fields. No critical appraisal (optional in scoping reviews). Synthesis by evidence mapping across five dimensions: study type (human-in-the-loop vs AI–human comparison), phase of scholarly communication, human role, epistemic biases reported, and quality and rigour metrics reported. Reporting follows PRISMA-ScR and PRISMA-S. Expected outcomes. A typology of human oversight configurations for generative AI in scholarly communication; an evidence map of the epistemic biases and quality metrics reported; identification of evidence gaps; and a basis for designing verifiable editorial evaluation workflows with generative AI.
